passages.text: School uniform should be abolished. Every morning, thousands of students put on the same shirt and tie, and every morning, they lose a small piece of who they are. Supporters of uniform claim it removes inequality, but this argument falls apart under scrutiny. A blazer does not erase the difference between a student who ate breakfast and one who did not. It does not close the gap between a household with broadband and one without. Uniform addresses the surface while ignoring the substance. If schools genuinely want equality, they should invest in breakfast clubs, free resources, and mental health support — not in policing the width of a trouser leg.

passages.text: The debate over screen time has become, ironically, the thing we spend most of our screen time arguing about. Parents worry. Teachers lecture. Headlines scream. Yet the conversation almost always misses the point. The issue is not how many hours a teenager spends online — it is what those hours contain. A student researching climate policy, teaching herself video editing, or organising a fundraiser through social media is not wasting time. She is developing skills that no textbook offers. Meanwhile, a student passively scrolling through thirty-second clips of strangers dancing may well be. The solution is not a blanket ban or a timer on the router. It is education: teaching young people to distinguish between consumption and creation, between noise and signal. We do not ban books because some of them are badly written. We teach students to read critically. The same principle applies to screens.

passages.text:
Dear Councillor Hargreaves,

I write to propose that your council introduces a Youth Community Service Programme, offering every sixteen-year-old in the borough twenty hours of supported volunteering before they leave school. This is not a punishment. It is an investment.

The evidence is difficult to ignore. A 2023 survey by the National Youth Agency found that young people who volunteer report higher confidence, stronger communication skills, and a clearer sense of purpose than those who do not. These are precisely the qualities employers say graduates lack. The programme would cost the council approximately twelve pounds per student — less than a single textbook — and would be staffed largely by existing community organisations who have already expressed interest.

Critics may argue that young people are already overstretched. This is a fair point, and one the programme addresses directly: volunteering slots would replace, not supplement, one afternoon of PSHE per half-term. No additional burden. No lost learning. Simply a different, arguably richer, form of education.

The young people of this borough are not the problem. They are the solution we keep forgetting to ask.

passages.text: They are closing Millfield Park. Not renovating it, not reimagining it — closing it. The swings will be removed. The benches will go. The patch of grass where my little brother learned to ride a bike will be sold to a property developer who has never set foot in this neighbourhood. The council says it is a financial decision. I say it is a failure of imagination. Parks do not generate profit on a spreadsheet, but they generate something far more valuable: community. Where will the Saturday morning joggers go? Where will the elderly residents sit when the sun comes out? Where will children play who do not have gardens of their own? These are not abstract questions. They are about real people, in a real place, who are about to lose something they cannot replace.

passages.text:
Open your wardrobe. Count the items you have worn in the last month. Now count the ones you have not. If you are honest, the second number is larger. This is the reality of fast fashion: a system designed not to clothe us but to convince us we are never clothed enough.

Every year, the average British household throws away thirty kilogrammes of clothing. Most of it ends up in landfill, where synthetic fibres will take two hundred years to decompose. The environmental cost is staggering, but the human cost is worse. In factories across South-East Asia, garment workers — many of them younger than you — sew twelve hours a day for wages that would not cover a single item on the rail they are producing.

The solution is not to stop buying clothes. It is to start thinking before you buy. One question is all it takes: will I still wear this in a year? If the answer is no, walk away. Your wardrobe — and the planet — will thank you.

passages.text:
Dear Editor,

Your recent editorial suggested that arts funding is a luxury we can no longer afford. With respect, this is precisely the kind of short-sighted thinking that impoverishes a community in ways no budget line can measure.

Consider the Riverside Youth Theatre, which your paper celebrated just eighteen months ago. Thirty teenagers from estates where unemployment runs at twice the national average spend their evenings learning to act, to collaborate, to stand in front of strangers and speak. Several have gone on to apprenticeships. Two are at university. One, who arrived unable to make eye contact, recently delivered a five-minute monologue to an audience of three hundred. None of this appears on a balance sheet.

Cutting arts funding saves money in the way that skipping meals saves time. It is technically true and profoundly foolish. The arts do not compete with essential services — they prevent the need for them. Every young person who finds purpose in a rehearsal room is one fewer young person the justice system will have to reach.

I urge you to reconsider your position, not as a matter of taste, but as a matter of investment.

passages.text: Last Tuesday, someone in this school did something extraordinary. They did not score the winning goal. They did not ace an exam. They sat down next to a student who was eating lunch alone and said, 'Can I join you?' That is it. Four words. No applause. No reward. And yet that one small act probably mattered more than anything else that happened in this building that day. We talk a lot about achievement in this school — grades, trophies, university offers. But kindness is not on the curriculum, and maybe it should be. Because the truth is, most of us will not remember our Year 11 test scores in ten years. But we will remember the person who noticed when we were struggling.

passages.text:
I am going to ask you for money. I know — no one likes that. But before you tune out, let me tell you about Priya. Priya is fourteen. She lives twenty minutes from this school, in a flat with no heating and a fridge that has been empty since Thursday. She goes to school hungry. She comes home to nothing. And she does this every single week, in one of the richest countries on earth.

Now, I am not here to make you feel guilty. Guilt is a terrible motivator — it fades by lunchtime. I am here because I believe this room is full of people who, when they understand a problem, want to fix it. Our local food bank serves four hundred families a month. Four hundred. That number has doubled since last year. They are not asking for sympathy. They are asking for tins of soup, packets of pasta, and the knowledge that someone, somewhere, has not forgotten them.

So here is what I am asking. Not your pity. Not even your money, if you do not have it. I am asking you to care. And if you do care, act. One tin. One packet. One decision to do something instead of nothing.

passages.text:
Five years ago, we walked into this school as strangers. We were eleven years old, and everything was too big — the corridors, the expectations, the blazers our parents had bought two sizes too large so we would grow into them. And we did grow into them. Not just the blazers.

We grew into people who can debate without shouting, who can fail an exam and sit the next one, who can lose a friend and learn what that word actually means. We did not always get it right. Some of us spent Year 9 pretending we did not care about anything, which is, of course, the most exhausting way of caring about everything. Some of us discovered we were braver than we thought. Some of us are still discovering it.

I am not going to stand here and say these were the best years of our lives. That would be a disservice to the years ahead. But I will say this: whatever comes next, we do not face it as the children who arrived here. We face it as the people this place helped us become. And that is worth something. That is worth everything.

So to the teachers who stayed late, to the friends who showed up, and to every single one of you who made it through to this moment — thank you. Not for making it easy. For making it matter.

passages.text:
Homework: Help or Hindrance?

Every evening, students across the country sit down to complete homework they did not ask for, on topics they covered hours ago, in a format that has not changed since their grandparents were at school. The question is not whether homework exists — it does, and it will. The question is whether it works.

Research suggests the answer is complicated. For younger students, the benefits are minimal. For older students, targeted revision can help — but only when it builds on what was taught, not when it fills time for the sake of routine. The problem with most homework is not the idea itself. It is the execution: worksheets photocopied from a textbook, due tomorrow, forgotten by Friday.

So what would better homework look like? It would be optional, purposeful, and designed around how students actually learn — not how schools have always operated.

passages.text:
Dear Councillor Osei,

I am writing to urge you to reconsider the proposed closure of Greenfield Library. As a student who has used this library every week for the past four years, I can tell you that its value cannot be measured in borrowing statistics alone.

The library is not simply a building that houses books. It is the only free, warm, quiet space in our community where young people can study without distraction. It is the place where my younger sister discovered she loved reading — not through a school lesson, but through a librarian who remembered her name and put aside books she thought my sister might enjoy. These are services that cannot be replicated by an app or a website.

I understand that the council faces difficult financial decisions, and I do not pretend that keeping the library open is free. But I would ask you to consider what closing it costs: not in pounds, but in opportunities lost, in young people who will have nowhere quiet to go, and in a community that loses its only shared indoor space.

I would welcome the opportunity to discuss this further and would be happy to attend a council meeting to represent the views of young library users.

Yours sincerely,
Jamie Okafor

The Ones Who Stay

Every town has them. The people who could leave but do not. The ones who run the youth club nobody funds, coach the football team nobody watches, and open the community centre on a Saturday morning when they could be anywhere else. They do not trend on social media. They do not win awards. And they almost certainly would not describe themselves as heroes.

In Ashford, that person is Denise Kowalski. For eleven years, Denise has run a free homework club from the back room of a church hall. She buys the biscuits herself. She prints the worksheets at home. When a student's family could not afford a calculator for their exam, Denise bought twelve and left them in a box by the door so no one had to ask.

The club has no website, no branding, and no funding. What it has is forty students a week, a waiting list of fifteen, and a stack of thank-you cards on Denise's mantlepiece that she claims she never reads but clearly does, because some of them are framed.

We spend a lot of time celebrating people who leave small towns to do extraordinary things. Perhaps we should spend more time celebrating the people who stay and make ordinary things extraordinary.

Should social media platforms raise their minimum age to sixteen? Many parents think so. The argument is simple: young teenagers are not emotionally equipped to handle the pressures of online life — the comparisons, the cruelty, the relentless performance of happiness.

It is a compelling case, and parts of it are undeniably true. But raising the age limit would not solve the problem. It would simply push it underground. A thirteen-year-old who is banned from a platform does not stop wanting to use it — they create a fake account, lie about their age, and access the same content without any of the safety features designed to protect them.

The better solution is not a higher wall. It is better education. Teach young people how to navigate social media critically, how to recognise manipulation, and how to log off when the screen starts to feel like a mirror they cannot stop checking. Ban them, and you lose the chance to guide them.

passages.text:
Every summer, the same debate resurfaces: are exams the fairest way to assess students? Those who defend the current system point to standardisation. An exam is the same for everyone. It is sat on the same day, under the same conditions, and marked against the same criteria. No one can buy an advantage. No parent can write it for them.

These are serious points, and they deserve to be taken seriously. Standardisation matters. But fairness is not the same as sameness. A two-hour exam on a Tuesday afternoon measures one thing: how well a student performs under pressure, on that day, in that format. It does not measure how well they understand the subject. It does not account for the student who thinks deeply but writes slowly, the student who panics in silence but thrives in discussion, or the student whose anxiety medication ran out the week before.

Coursework is not perfect either. It is vulnerable to plagiarism, to unequal access to resources, and to the quiet advantage of having a parent who went to university. But the answer is not to choose one system over the other. It is to use both — to build an assessment model that captures different kinds of intelligence, not just the kind that performs well under a clock.
passages.label: Model B — Opinion article on exams versus coursework

passages.text:
The case against zoos writes itself. Animals bred in captivity, pacing enclosures a fraction of their natural range, performing for crowds who have paid for entertainment and called it education. It is an uncomfortable image, and it should be.

But discomfort is not the same as a conclusion. The question is not whether zoos are ideal — they are not — but whether the world is better with them or without them. And here, the evidence complicates the outrage.

Consider the Arabian oryx, hunted to extinction in the wild by 1972. Today, over a thousand roam the deserts of Oman, every one of them descended from animals kept alive in zoos. Consider the California condor, reduced to twenty-two individuals in 1987, now numbering over five hundred thanks to captive breeding programmes that no wildlife reserve could have delivered alone. These are not edge cases. They are proof that zoos, at their best, do something no other institution can.

The honest position is not pro-zoo or anti-zoo. It is this: zoos as entertainment are indefensible. Zoos as conservation are essential. The task is not to abolish them but to hold them to the higher standard — and to close the ones that fail it.

passages.text:
The Canteen Problem

Let me describe a typical school lunch. A limp sandwich in a plastic triangle. A bag of crisps. A carton of juice with more sugar than a dessert. Total cost: three pounds fifty. Nutritional value: questionable.

This is not an exaggeration. This is Tuesday. And Wednesday. And most of the week for thousands of students who rely on their school canteen for their only hot meal of the day.

The solution is not complicated. Schools that have switched to freshly prepared meals report that students concentrate better in afternoon lessons, behave better in corridors, and — here is the part that surprises people — actually eat more, not less. Good food is not a luxury. It is infrastructure. You would not expect a student to learn in a classroom with no heating. Why do we expect them to learn on a lunch that would not pass a health inspection?

passages.text:
Dear Transport Secretary,

I am writing to propose that all public transport in England should be free for under-eighteens. This is not charity. It is strategy.

At present, a return bus fare in most towns costs between three and five pounds. For a student travelling to school five days a week, that is fifteen to twenty-five pounds — money that many families simply do not have. The result is predictable: students walk dangerous routes, miss enrichment activities, and turn down work experience placements because they cannot afford to get there. We are not failing to invest in young people. We are charging them for the privilege of being invested in.

The counterargument is cost. Free travel is expensive. But expensive compared to what? The average cost of a young person not in education, employment, or training is estimated at fifty-six thousand pounds over their lifetime in lost tax revenue and increased welfare payments. A bus pass costs three hundred. The maths is not complicated.

Free transport would not solve every problem young people face. But it would remove one of the quietest, most persistent barriers to opportunity — the one we barely notice because it costs so little for those of us who can afford it.
passages.label: Model B — Letter on public transport for under-eighteens

passages.text:
The Case for Doing Nothing

Here is an experiment. Put your phone in a drawer for twenty-four hours. Not on silent — in a drawer, where you cannot see it, where the screen cannot light up and pull your attention sideways every forty-five seconds. Then notice what happens.

You will be bored. Properly, uncomfortably, almost painfully bored. You will reach for something that is not there. You will check the time on a clock you forgot you owned. And then, somewhere around hour six, something else will happen. You will think. Not react, not scroll, not consume — think. A slow, unprompted thought that arrives because, for the first time in months, there is space for it.

I am not anti-technology. I use my phone for work, for music, for staying in contact with people I love. But I have started to notice that the phone does not wait to be used. It uses me. It decides when I am bored. It fills silences I did not ask it to fill. And the more it does, the less I am able to tolerate the quiet — which is exactly where the best ideas, the deepest rest, and the most honest conversations live.

This is not a call to abandon your phone. It is a call to reclaim the thing your phone has quietly taken: your ability to be alone with your own mind and find that it is enough.
passages.label: Model C — Magazine article on digital detox

passages.text:
Beyond the Classroom

School trips are often dismissed as days off in disguise. A coach ride, a gift shop, and a worksheet no one fills in. But this view misses the point entirely.

The best school trips do something no classroom can: they place learning in the real world. A student who has read about trench warfare understands it differently after standing in a preserved dugout in northern France. A student who has studied river processes sees them differently after measuring the velocity of a stream with their own hands. These experiences are not substitutes for teaching. They are extensions of it.

Of course, trips cost money, and not every family can afford them. This is a real concern and one that schools must address with subsidies, fundraising, and creative planning. But the solution is to make trips accessible, not to abandon them. Cutting trips because some students cannot afford them is like removing books from a library because some people do not read.

School trips should not be optional extras. They should be part of the curriculum — funded, planned, and treated as seriously as any lesson.

passages.text:
I want to talk about a waiting list. Not the kind you join for trainers or concert tickets — the kind a fourteen-year-old joins when they tell someone, for the first time, that they are not okay.

In this country, the average wait for a young person to access mental health support is twelve weeks. Twelve weeks. That is an entire school term. Imagine telling a student with a broken arm to come back in September. You would not do it. You would not even consider it. And yet, when the injury is invisible, we ask children to wait — and we call it a system.

I am not here to blame anyone. I know funding is limited. I know that the people who work in these services are exhausted, understaffed, and doing extraordinary work with insufficient resources. This is not a failure of individuals. It is a failure of priority.

What I am asking for is simple. Not perfection. Not a miracle. Just the acknowledgement that a child who asks for help deserves an answer before they stop asking. Because the most dangerous waiting list is the one young people take themselves off — not because they got better, but because they gave up.

Thank you.

passages.text:
Dear Editor,

Your recent article questioned whether compulsory volunteering for school students would be worth the disruption. Allow me to suggest that the question is back to front. The real question is whether we can afford the disruption of not doing it.

We live in a society where young people are routinely described as disconnected, entitled, and disengaged — usually by adults who have given them nothing to connect to, no entitlement worth having, and nothing to engage with beyond a screen and a syllabus. Compulsory community service is not the solution to youth apathy. But it is an answer to adult complacency.

The evidence from programmes abroad is consistent. In countries where community service is a graduation requirement, young people report greater civic confidence, stronger empathy, and a more optimistic view of their community. These are not soft outcomes. They are the foundation of a functioning democracy.

The objection I hear most often is that compulsory volunteering is a contradiction — that forcing generosity defeats the purpose. It is a neat argument, and it sounds right. But it rests on the assumption that every teenager who has never volunteered has freely chosen not to. Most have not. Most have simply never been asked, never been shown what community means outside a textbook, and never discovered that they are good at something their report card has no column for.

Compulsion is not the enemy of genuine engagement. It is often the introduction to it. We compel children to study mathematics, and some of them discover they love it. We could do the same with service — and some of them would discover they love that too.

Yours faithfully,
R. Chowdhury
